title: MIME Parameter Value and Encoded Word Extensions
summary: Extends the way MIME parameter values, such as filenames, are written so they can use other character sets and be split across several pieces. It also extends encoded words to name the language of the text. It replaces RFC 2184.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2231 extends MIME so parameter values can include text from other character sets, identify a language, and continue across several pieces. It also adds language information to encoded words in message headers.

subtitle: MIME parameters can carry other character sets, language information, and long values split into numbered parts.

tldr.problem: MIME parameter values can be too long for reliable header folding, are restricted to US-ASCII, and do not identify the language of displayed text.
tldr.mechanism: Numbered asterisk suffixes split long values into ordered pieces. An extended value marks a character set and language, then uses percent-encoded octets; encoded words can also include a language tag.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2231 obsoletes RFC 2184 and updates RFCs 2045, 2047, and 2183. It advises using these extensions only when needed.

today: RFC 2231 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2184 and updates RFC 2045, RFC 2047, and RFC 2183. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 2231.

sections.title: Limits of MIME Parameter Values
sections.content:
MIME parameters appear in fields such as Content-Type and Content-Disposition; an attachment filename is one example. Header folding can damage long values, and the usual header syntax is limited to 7-bit US-ASCII.

Character-set information alone may not tell a program how to display or read text. RFC 2231 adds ways to express long values, non-ASCII data, and language information while retaining compatible syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME headers need a way to carry long names and text outside basic US-ASCII. They can also need a language label when software displays or reads the text.

sections.title: Splitting Long Parameter Values
sections.content:
A continuation uses an asterisk and a decimal section number after the parameter name, such as filename*0 and filename*1. Numbering starts at zero, increases by one, and cannot contain gaps or leading zeros.

The reader reconstructs the value by joining the sections in order. The quote marks belong to the header syntax and are not part of the value; continued parts may be quoted or unquoted.
sections.plainLanguage: A long value can be divided into numbered sections. Put the sections back in number order to recover the original value.

sections.title: Character Set, Language and Encoded Octets
sections.content:
A parameter name ending in an asterisk marks an extended value. The value begins with a character-set name, a single quote, a language tag, another single quote, and then the text. A percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits represents an octet.

The character-set or language field may be empty, but both quote separators remain. Continuations can combine encoded and unencoded pieces, but character-set and language information appear only at the start of the whole value.
sections.plainLanguage: An extended value can state its character set and language before its text. Special octets use a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits, and the first continued part carries this information.

sections.title: Language Tags in Encoded Words
sections.content:
RFC 2047 encoded words carry non-US-ASCII text in message headers. RFC 2231 adds an optional language tag after the character-set name, separated by an asterisk.

The language is useful because encoded words are mainly intended for display. The RFC prefers future character sets with inline language information when those become available, because they can change language within a string.
sections.plainLanguage: An encoded word can state both its character set and its language. This gives a display program more information about the text.

sections.title: Grammar and IMAP Handling
sections.content:
The revised MIME grammar allows regular parameters, extended parameters, and numbered sections. In an extended section, a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits represents encoded octets.

For IMAP4, servers SHOULD decode parameter continuations when producing BODY and BODYSTRUCTURE fetch attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal MIME grammar now recognizes extended values and numbered continuations. IMAP4 servers should join continued values when returning the specified body information.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it does not introduce security issues beyond those already present in electronic mail and fully conforming MIME implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports no new security issues beyond existing email and MIME concerns.
